en: Mayon Volcano has a perfect conical shape because its highly viscous lava cools and hardens quickly before flowing far down the slopes.
The Sierra Madre mountain range reduces typhoon wind speeds in Luzon because the massive peaks force storms to expend energy climbing over them.
Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide to become slightly acidic, which slowly dissolves the limestone of Puerto Princesa to carve its massive underground river cave.
The southwest monsoon brings heavy rain to western Philippines because moisture-laden winds from the South China Sea cool and condense when hitting mountains.
The Pasig River occasionally flows backward from Laguna de Bay to Manila Bay because strong ocean tides push seawater upstream during high tide.
Geothermal plants in Tiwi generate electricity because underground magma heats groundwater into high-pressure steam, which then spins turbines to produce power.
Tubbataha Reef supports vibrant corals because its clear, shallow waters allow maximum sunlight to reach the photosynthetic algae living inside coral polyps.
Palawan hosts unique mammals like the bearcat because it was connected to Borneo by a land bridge during the Ice Age, allowing animal migration.
The Banaue Rice Terraces prevent mountain soil erosion because ancient stone walls trap rainwater on steep slopes, creating flat, stable ponds for growing rice.
Bukidnon produces abundant pineapples because past volcanic eruptions deposited ash that weathered into deep, mineral-rich soil, providing essential nutrients for the crops.
The Kuroshio Current warms the eastern Philippine seas because it transports massive volumes of hot, equatorial water northward along the Pacific coastline.
Lake Taal formed when powerful volcanic eruptions collapsed the ground into a massive caldera, which subsequently filled with rainwater and river runoff.
